alt: Encoding, storage and retrieval are linked. Encoding can be acoustic, visual or semantic. Long-term memory has three types: episodic (personal experiences), semantic (facts) and procedural (skills). Clive Wearing lost most episodic memory but kept the procedural skill of playing the piano.
caption: Episodic, semantic and procedural memories are stored differently, and can be lost separately.

alt: A U-shaped curve of chance of recall against position in a list. Early words show a primacy effect because they were rehearsed into the long-term store; the last words show a recency effect because they were still in the short-term store; middle words are recalled worst. Cards give the variables, conclusion and evaluation.
caption: Primacy from long-term memory, recency from short-term memory: evidence for separate stores.

after: ## Memory as an active process: Bartlett
alt: Three pages get shorter as an unfamiliar folk tale is reproduced again and again, with some lines changed. The changes: shortened, unfamiliar details omitted and details transformed into familiar forms. Schemas fill gaps and effort after meaning makes the story fit what we know. An evaluation note follows.
caption: Each recall rebuilds the story to fit our schemas: shorter, simpler, more familiar.

after: ## Factors affecting the accuracy of memory
alt: Two interference rows: proactive, where old learning disrupts new (an old PIN), and retroactive, where new learning disrupts old (last term's timetable). Cards cover context, where divers recalled better in the same environment as learning, and false memories, where suggestion produced recall of invented events.
caption: Interference, a change of context and suggestion can all make recall inaccurate.
